neighbors.heading: the mind that runs
neighbors.text: Today the mind was a monkey in the trees, grabbing one branch, then the next. Sikhs know that restless mind well. Guru Nanak's Japji, the morning prayer, puts the whole task in a few words: conquer the mind, and you conquer the world. In Gurbani the mind is spoken to again and again, gently, and called back home.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs steady the mind by remembering the one God's Name, and the soul is real and returns to God. The Abhidhamma sees mind as moments arising and passing, with no fixed self behind them and no creator to return to.
neighbors.shared: a restless mind can be steadied, one moment at a time.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji, pauri 28, Ang 6 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: new every morning
neighbors.text: Today a bad mood was a page in a flip book, and the next page isn't drawn yet. Christians know a fresh page too. In Lamentations, a book written in grief, the poet says of God: "his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness." Yesterday's worst page doesn't have to be the last one.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, the new start comes from a faithful God whose mercy doesn't change. For the Abhidhamma, the newness is in the mind itself, always arising and passing, with no creator needed for the next moment to come.
neighbors.shared: the next page isn't written yet.

neighbors.heading: the one who craves more
neighbors.text: Today greed was a torrent, carrying things away: a cart at eleven at night, an argument that has to be won. The Stoic philosopher Seneca saw the same current. In a letter to a friend he wrote: "It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor." Enough isn't a number. It's a way of holding.
neighbors.difference: Seneca answers craving with reason and a simple life, so a person stays free. The Abhidhamma goes finer: greed, wrong view and conceit are one family, each a moment of the mind holding on, seen so it can be let go.
neighbors.shared: wanting less can feel like having more.

neighbors.heading: the root of evils
neighbors.text: Today greed reached wider than money: any holding on, even to being right. Catholics name it too. A letter of Saint Paul warns: "For the desire of money is the root of all evils." The Church counts avarice among the capital sins, the roots other wrongs grow from, and pride sits on that list as well.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, greed is a sin that turns the heart from God and neighbor, healed by grace and generosity. For the Abhidhamma, greed is a root of suffering in the mind, seen clearly and let go, with no God to turn back to.
neighbors.shared: a closed hand can learn to open.
neighbors.sources: 1 Timothy 6:10 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1866 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the discipline of words
neighbors.text: Today right speech was a moment: the mind turning away from a lie it could have told. Hindus guard the tongue too. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna names words that cause no distress, that are true, kind and helpful, as a discipline of speech, a quiet kind of tapas, right alongside study of the sacred texts.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, disciplined speech is an offering on the way to God, taught by Krishna. In the Abhidhamma, abstaining is a mental factor that arises in a single moment, with no God to offer it to.
neighbors.shared: a word held back can be a gift.

neighbors.heading: keep thy tongue
neighbors.text: Today the right word was a turning away, in the very moment it mattered. A psalm Jews sing says it plainly: "Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile. Depart from evil, and do good." The rabbis built whole teachings on guarding speech, and they warn against gossip even when it's true.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, guarding speech is part of keeping God's commandments, a way of life before God. For the Abhidhamma, it's a factor of mind arising in a moment, with no commandment-giver behind it.
neighbors.shared: what we don't say can protect someone.

neighbors.heading: the company you keep
neighbors.text: Today who you spend the afternoon with became something the mind leans on. Christians have a proverb for it: "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed." Friends tip a person one way or the other, and Christian communities gather partly for that reason, to lean on one another well.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, good company helps a person grow toward God, and fellowship is shared in Christ. For the Abhidhamma, a friend is one strong condition among many, alongside food, weather and a quiet room, with no God at the center.
neighbors.shared: who we sit with shapes who we become.

neighbors.heading: the perfume seller
neighbors.text: Today a friend was a strong support, tipping the mind one way or the other. The Prophet Muhammad gave a picture of it. A good companion is like a perfume seller: he may give you some, you may buy some, or you'll at least enjoy the scent. A bad one is like a blacksmith's bellows: it may burn your clothes, or you'll leave with a bad smell.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, good company helps a person remember and obey God. For the Abhidhamma, a friend is a condition among others, food, weather, a place, that leans on the mind, with no Creator in the picture.
neighbors.shared: a good friend leaves something good on you.
neighbors.sources: hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 5534 and Sahih Muslim 2628 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: doing good on earth
neighbors.text: Today the bodhisattva turned the wish for freedom outward, to include everyone. Catholics know a saint who said something close. Near the end of her short life, Thérèse of Lisieux told her sisters she wanted to spend her heaven doing good on earth. The Church teaches that the saints keep praying for the living, still part of one family.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, the saints help by praying to God, who alone saves, and heaven is life with him. The bodhisattva vows to work for every being's awakening, life after life, on a path with no creator God at its end.
neighbors.shared: one life can be spent on everyone's good.
neighbors.sources: Thérèse of Lisieux, last conversations, 1897 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 956 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the good of all
neighbors.text: Today the bodhisattva's wish grew wide enough to hold everyone. Sikhs end their Ardas, the prayer said at gurdwaras and at home, with the same wide wish: Nanak, through the Name may spirits rise, and by your will, may all be blessed. Sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Not just my family. Everyone.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs ask the one God for the good of all, trusting that it comes by God's will. The bodhisattva makes a vow to work for every being's freedom himself, across many lives, with no creator to ask.
neighbors.shared: the prayer isn't finished until it includes everyone.

neighbors.heading: the soul is pure
neighbors.text: Today a precious statue sat by the road in dirty rags, and people walked right past it. Jews begin the day with a blessing that sees under the rags. The Talmud gives its words: my God, the soul you placed within me is pure. You created it, you breathed it into me, and you keep it within me.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, the pure soul is God's gift, and it returns to God. Buddha-nature isn't a soul or self given by a creator; Buddhists read it as a seed of awakening, or as the mind's own nature, already whole.
neighbors.shared: under everything, something good stays clean.
neighbors.sources: Talmud, Berakhot 60b (paraphrase) · the morning blessing Elohai Neshamah

neighbors.heading: the potato in the cellar
neighbors.text: Today the good in every person was gold in filth, covered but never lost. The psychologist Carl Rogers described something like it. He remembered potatoes stored in a dark cellar, sending pale sprouts toward a small far window. People, he said, carry the same pull toward growth, even when hard years have covered it over.
neighbors.difference: Rogers spoke of a natural tendency in living things to grow, a fact of nature, not a path. Buddha-nature points toward awakening itself, and some Buddhists read it as already whole, waiting to be uncovered.
neighbors.shared: something in everyone keeps turning toward the light.
neighbors.sources: Carl Rogers, A Way of Being, 1980 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: with wisdom
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha was a doctor, fitting the medicine to each patient. The Qur'an asks for care in how a message is shared, too: "Call unto the way of thy Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation, and reason with them in the better way." How something is said, and to whom, matters as much as saying it.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the message itself stays one and the same; wisdom shapes only how it's offered. The Lotus goes further: even the teachings can be means fitted to the listener, like the carts promised to the children.
neighbors.shared: the kindest teacher speaks so you can hear.

neighbors.heading: meeting people where they are
neighbors.text: Today a teaching was a tool, shaped to the person in front of it. The Bhagavad Gita says something close. Krishna advises the wise not to unsettle people who are still attached to their work, but to keep working alongside them and lead by example. Hindu teachers speak of fitting a teaching to a student's readiness.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the teacher is Krishna, whom many Hindus worship as God himself. In the Lotus, the Buddha is an awakened teacher, not a creator, and even his teachings are means, like a raft put down once the river is crossed.
neighbors.shared: a good teacher starts where the student stands.

neighbors.heading: honest work
neighbors.text: Today a great sutra opened with chores: a bowl, a walk, clean feet. Sikhs see the holy in ordinary work too. Tradition remembers Guru Nanak farming his fields at Kartarpur. And Gurbani says: one who eats what they earn by honest work, and gives some of it away, knows the path.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs earn by their own work while remembering God's Name, and share what they earn. The Buddha lived as a monk on gifts, walking for alms, and the sutra's ordinary morning is about full attention, with no God it's offered to.
neighbors.shared: the everyday is where the path is walked.

neighbors.heading: whatsoever ye do
neighbors.text: Today the Buddha did an ordinary morning completely, then sat down. Christians are told to bring that same wholeness to chores. A letter of Saint Paul says: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." Dishes, emails and the walk to work all count.
neighbors.difference: For Christians, ordinary work is done for the Lord, as service offered to God. The sutra's morning offers nothing to anyone; each act is simply done fully, and the teaching is shown before it's spoken.
neighbors.shared: nothing done with your whole heart is small.

neighbors.heading: like a vine
neighbors.text: Today the gift went out and didn't come back on a string. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote something close in his private notebook. Some people do a kindness and keep the account, he said. Better to be like a vine that bears its grapes and asks for nothing more, then bears again next season.
neighbors.difference: Marcus gives because doing good is human nature, the way a vine makes grapes. The sutra lets go further: no fixed giver, no gift, no receiver to hold on to, and so the merit can't be measured.
neighbors.shared: a gift is finished when it leaves your hand.

neighbors.heading: the left hand
neighbors.text: Today the giver was asked not to lean on the gift, or on the picture of themselves giving it. Jesus said something close in the Sermon on the Mount: "But when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth." Give quietly, without keeping score.
neighbors.difference: Jesus adds that the Father who sees in secret will repay: God sees every hidden gift. The sutra asks the giver to hold no idea of self, gift or receiver at all, and there is no God keeping the account.
neighbors.shared: the best gifts don't wait for a thank-you.

neighbors.heading: speaking of it together
neighbors.text: Today holy ground was wherever the teaching is explained, out loud, between people. Hindus know that kind of ground. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna describes devotees who keep their minds on him, teaching one another and speaking of him together, and finding joy and contentment in it. Hindus call such gatherings satsang, good company.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the talk is of Krishna, loved as God, and the joy is devotion. The sutra honors the teaching itself, a verse of four lines, and wherever it's explained the ground becomes like a shrine, with no God at the center.
neighbors.shared: a real conversation can make any room holy.

neighbors.heading: two at a table
neighbors.text: Today a kitchen table became a shrine because something good was explained there. The rabbis said it about Torah. In Pirkei Avot, Rabbi Hananiah ben Teradion teaches: when two sit together and words of Torah pass between them, the Shekhinah, God's presence, rests among them. No synagogue required. Two people and the words are enough.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, it's God's own presence that rests among those who study. The sutra speaks of the Buddha or a worthy disciple being where the teaching is, and honors the teaching itself, not a creator God.
neighbors.shared: words shared well can make ordinary ground holy.
neighbors.sources: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 3:2 (paraphrase; 3:3 in some prayer books)

neighbors.heading: no thought for the morrow
neighbors.text: Today the future mind couldn't be grasped: what's here is only planning, happening now. Jesus said something close in the Sermon on the Mount: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." Today is enough to carry.
neighbors.difference: Jesus tells his listeners they need not worry because the Father knows what they need. The sutra's reason is different: no mind, past, present or future, is a fixed thing to hold, and no one is holding it for you.
neighbors.shared: tomorrow's worry doesn't have to live in today.

neighbors.heading: if God wills
neighbors.text: Today tomorrow's mind slipped through the hand: it isn't here yet. The Qur'an has words that let tomorrow stay open: "And say not of anything: Lo! I shall do that tomorrow, Except if Allah will." Muslims say insha'Allah, if God wills, about plans large and small, from a trip to a coffee.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, tomorrow belongs to God's will, and plans are made trusting him. The sutra simply finds that future mind can't be grasped, with no Creator holding the days.
neighbors.shared: plans are held loosely, and the day is lived.

neighbors.heading: unprofitable servants
neighbors.text: Today the good was made, then not grabbed, like a river nobody owns. Jesus told his disciples something close: "When you shall have done all these things that are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done that which we ought to do." The Church teaches that even our merits are God's gifts.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, merit is real before God and comes from his grace, so the glory goes to him. The sutra says merit is gained but not held, because no fixed self is there to keep it, and no God gives it.
neighbors.shared: good done well doesn't need to be counted.
neighbors.sources: Luke 17:10 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2008–2011 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: in ego they give
neighbors.text: Today the bodhisattva didn't take hold of merit. Sikhs watch for the same grip. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak sings of a life run by haumai, ego: in ego they give, in ego they take. And Guru Angad adds that ego is a deep illness, yet its cure lies within it too.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, ego is cured by God's grace and the Guru's word, by remembering the Name. The sutra loosens the grip by seeing no fixed self at all, with no God's grace needed.
neighbors.shared: the giving is lighter when the 'I' steps back.

neighbors.heading: like a breath
neighbors.text: Today the world was dew, a bubble, a flash of lightning: real, and passing. A psalm Jews sing says it of a human life: "Man is like unto a breath; his days are as a shadow that passeth away." The Hebrew poets didn't call life fake. They called it brief, and worth noticing because it is.
neighbors.difference: The psalm sets passing human life beside an eternal God who still takes notice of us. The sutra sees everything made as passing, with no eternal maker behind it, and seeing that clearly frees the mind.
neighbors.shared: knowing it passes makes the moment dearer.

neighbors.heading: a river of events
neighbors.text: Today the sutra's last verse pointed at dew on the glass, gone before the keys are found. The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote something close in his private notebook: time is like a river of things happening, a strong current. As soon as one thing is seen, it's carried off, and another takes its place.
neighbors.difference: Marcus used this to steady himself and live by reason, accepting nature's course. The sutra uses it to loosen all grasping toward awakening, while warning that passing doesn't mean nothing.
neighbors.shared: everything passes, and this moment is still here.

items.lessonTitle: The jewel in the coat (Kern ch. 8)

neighbors.heading: nearer than you knew
neighbors.text: Today a man wandered poor with a jewel stitched into his coat. The Qur'an speaks of nearness a person forgets too. God says of each human being: "We know what his soul whispereth to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." What a person searches far for may be closer than breath.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the One who is near is God, the Creator, always distinct from his creation. In the Lotus, the jewel is the aim of awakening the Buddha placed in his disciples, and no creator is involved.
neighbors.shared: what you're looking for may already be close.

neighbors.heading: walking over the gold
neighbors.text: Today the treasure was already in the coat. A Hindu Upanishad tells a story close to it. People who don't know the land walk back and forth over hidden gold every day and never find it. In the same way, it says, beings pass through the deepest truth day after day, unaware it's there.
neighbors.difference: The Upanishad teaches that the treasure is the Self, the atman, one with Brahman. Buddhists teach that there is no fixed self; the Lotus's jewel is the aim of awakening, a gift waiting to be noticed.
neighbors.shared: the treasure is already where we walk.

neighbors.heading: why call her less?
neighbors.text: Today a young girl awakened faster than the doubters could finish their doubt. Guru Nanak answered a doubt like theirs. In Asa di Var he sings that woman bears us, man is born of woman, and kings are born of her. So why call her less? Sikh women and men can lead the prayer and read from the Guru Granth Sahib.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak's words honor women as equal before the one God, in this very life. The Lotus story shows the girl's body changing before she awakens, which Buddhists read in more than one way.
neighbors.shared: nobody gets to say who can reach the deepest truth.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Asa di Var, Ang 473 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: neither male nor female
neighbors.text: Today a girl from the sea surprised the wise men who said she couldn't. Saint Paul wrote words some Christians hear the same way: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus." Churches still differ on what it means for women's roles in ministry.
neighbors.difference: Paul's oneness is in Christ, received through faith and baptism. The naga princess reaches awakening through deep understanding of the teaching, in an instant, with no savior involved.
neighbors.shared: nobody is shut out by the body they were born in.

neighbors.heading: never just a means
neighbors.text: Today a monk bowed to everyone he met, even those throwing stones. The philosopher Immanuel Kant reached a rule from reason alone: treat every person, yourself included, always as an end in their own right, never merely as a tool for something else. Worth isn't earned by being nice. It comes with being a person.
neighbors.difference: Kant grounds each person's worth in their power to reason and choose. Never Disparaging bowed because he saw in each person a future Buddha, someone on the path to awakening.
neighbors.shared: every person you meet is worth a bow.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: pray for them
neighbors.text: Today a monk called back his blessing from a distance, out of reach of the sticks. Jesus asked the same of his followers: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you." The Church teaches that every person's dignity comes from being made in God's image.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, each person's dignity comes from God, who made them and loves them. The monk honored each person as a future Buddha, someone who will awaken, without pointing to a creator.
neighbors.shared: you can keep blessing, even from a step away.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 5:44 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1700 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the elephant's cry
neighbors.text: Today Avalokiteshvara heard every cry and came. Hindus tell of a cry heard, too. In the Bhagavata Purana, Gajendra, a king of elephants, is caught by a crocodile in a lake. His strength runs out. He lifts a lotus in his trunk and calls to God, and Vishnu comes and frees him.
neighbors.difference: For many Hindus, Vishnu who answers is the Supreme God. Avalokiteshvara is a bodhisattva, a being of compassion on the path to awakening, honored but not a creator.
neighbors.shared: a cry for help can reach someone who listens.
neighbors.sources: Bhagavata Purana, book 8, the story of Gajendra (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: nigh unto all
neighbors.text: Today a whole list of bad nights, fire, flood, chains, each answered when someone called out. A psalm Jews pray every day says it simply: "The LORD is nigh unto all them that call upon Him, to all that call upon Him in truth." No special words required. A true call is enough.
neighbors.difference: Jews call directly on the one God, with no go-between. Avalokiteshvara is a bodhisattva, not God, who comes in many forms to help beings toward freedom.
neighbors.shared: calling out in trouble is never wasted.

items.lessonTitle: I'm sick because the world is sick

neighbors.heading: one member suffers
neighbors.text: Today Vimalakirti said he was sick because the world is sick, the way a parent hurts with a sick child. Saint Paul wrote to a church about the same closeness: "And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it."
neighbors.difference: Paul speaks of the church as the body of Christ, joined through him. Vimalakirti's sickness reaches out to all beings, out of great compassion, as a bodhisattva's choice.
neighbors.shared: love means your pain is never only yours.

neighbors.heading: one body
neighbors.text: Today a sick man said his illness came from compassion. The Prophet Muhammad gave a picture of that closeness. In their love, mercy and kindness to one another, believers are like one body: when one part aches, the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever.
neighbors.difference: The hadith speaks of the believers, bound together by faith in God. Vimalakirti's compassion reaches out to all beings and is part of a bodhisattva's path, without a Creator at its center.
neighbors.shared: when one hurts, those who love them feel it.
neighbors.sources: hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 6011 and Sahih Muslim 2586 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: words that fall short
neighbors.text: Today a finger pointed at the moon, and the finger was needed, but it wasn't the moon. The Church says something close about speaking of God. The Catechism teaches that human words always fall short of the mystery of God, yet they really point to him. Tradition says Thomas Aquinas, near the end, called his writings straw.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, God himself speaks through Scripture and in Christ, so the words carry his revelation. For the Lankavatara, the moon is the truth of awakening, not a God, and words only point the way.
neighbors.shared: words matter, and they point past themselves.

neighbors.heading: beyond thinking
neighbors.text: Today words were a finger, and the moon was further on. Guru Nanak begins the Japji the same way. By thinking, he sings, the One can't be reached, even if a person thinks a hundred thousand times. By silence, inner quiet doesn't come either. The path, he says, is walking in the Hukam, the will.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the Guru's word, the Gurbani, is the living Guru, and it leads to the one God. For the Lankavatara, words point to the truth, and there is no creator to reach.
neighbors.shared: the words are a door, not the room.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji, pauri 1, Ang 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one leads to another
neighbors.text: Today every act left a seed, waiting to ripen. The rabbis saw the same chain. In Pirkei Avot, Ben Azzai teaches: run to do even a small good deed, and flee from wrong, because one good deed leads to another, and one wrong leads to another. The reward of a mitzvah is another mitzvah.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, a mitzvah is a commandment of God, and the chain is a life lived before him. Yogacara's seeds ripen by cause and condition in the mind's storehouse, with no commandment-giver.
neighbors.shared: today's small choice plants tomorrow's habit.

neighbors.heading: never so little scar
neighbors.text: Today seeds sat in a storehouse until a tired evening ripened them. The psychologist William James wrote about habit the same way: "Every smallest stroke of virtue or of vice leaves its never so little scar." We are spinning our own fates, he said. Small acts, repeated, become who we are.
neighbors.difference: James explained habit through the nervous system, inside one lifetime. Yogacara teachers described a storehouse of seeds in the mind, a stream that some held continues from life to life.
neighbors.shared: small acts, repeated, shape a life.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology, ch. 4, "Habit" (William James 1890)

neighbors.heading: counting praise
neighbors.text: Today the breath was counted to ten, and losing count meant simply starting again. Muslims count too. The Prophet Muhammad taught his daughter Fatima to say, at bedtime, glory be to God thirty-three times, praise be to God thirty-three times, and God is greatest thirty-four times. Many count on their fingers or a string of beads.
neighbors.difference: Muslims count words of praise to God, and the counting is itself remembrance of him. Zen counts plain numbers on the breath, with no words of praise, and the count is meant to be put down later.
neighbors.shared: counting can gently bring a wandering mind home.
neighbors.sources: hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 3705 and Sahih Muslim 2727 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: bead by bead
neighbors.text: Today a number tied a wandering mind to something simple. Hindus know that rope. In japa, a person repeats a mantra or a name of God, moving one bead at a time along a mala. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that among offerings, he is japa, the quiet repeating.
neighbors.difference: In japa, what's repeated is a sacred name or mantra, offered to God. Counting breaths uses plain numbers, no name and no God, and it's a first step, dropped when the mind steadies.
neighbors.shared: when the mind wanders, coming back is the practice.

neighbors.heading: walking in the will
neighbors.text: Today an old poem said the way isn't hard, if we stop grabbing one side and pushing away the other. Sikhs know a way to set that quiet war down. The Japji asks how a person can become true, and answers: by walking in the Hukam, the will, written with you from the start.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the Hukam is the will of the one God, and peace comes from accepting it. The poem trusts the mind, just as it is, to meet the way, with no will above it.
neighbors.shared: peace starts where the fight with what is ends.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Japji, pauri 1, Ang 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: content in whatsoever state
neighbors.text: Today rain on the day of a picnic was just rain, without the war piled on top. Saint Paul, writing from prison, said something close: "for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." He says he learned it, which means it took practice.
neighbors.difference: Paul's contentment rests on Christ, who, he writes, gives him strength. The poem's trust is in the mind itself, already enough to meet the way, without picking and choosing.
neighbors.shared: contentment can be learned, a day at a time.

neighbors.heading: into the woods
neighbors.text: Today a herdsman parted endless grasses, looking for an ox, and found only the evening cicadas. Henry David Thoreau went looking too. In Walden he wrote: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach."
neighbors.difference: Thoreau searched outward, in nature and a simpler life. The oxherding preface says the ox was never really missing; the herdsman only turned away from his own nature.
neighbors.shared: admitting you're searching is the first honest step.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden, "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For" (Thoreau)

neighbors.heading: the restless heart
neighbors.text: Today the search began, worn out, with nothing found yet. Saint Augustine began his Confessions in that same place, speaking to God: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." The restlessness itself, he thought, was a sign of where home is.
neighbors.difference: For Augustine, the heart rests in God, who made it and seeks it first. In the oxherding pictures, the ox is often read as one's own true nature, never really lost, with no God to find.
neighbors.shared: a restless heart is already looking for home.

neighbors.heading: for the good of the world
neighbors.text: Today the search ended not on a mountain but in town, among neighbors, with open hands. The Bhagavad Gita says something close. Krishna points to King Janaka, who reached perfection through action, not by leaving the world. Act, he says, with the good of the world in view.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, action is offered to Krishna, without craving its fruits, as a duty done for God. The oxherd simply walks among people, with no duty to keep and nothing to offer, and trees bloom around him.
neighbors.shared: wisdom comes back to the kitchen table.

neighbors.heading: don't stand apart
neighbors.text: Today the oxherd came back to the market, buying vegetables and listening to a neighbor. Hillel taught something close in Pirkei Avot: do not separate yourself from the community. Jewish life keeps holiness close to the table and the street, where prayer is often said with others and help is done among neighbors.
neighbors.difference: Hillel speaks of staying with the Jewish community, living by Torah together before God. The oxherd returns after awakening, with no commandments, simply as ordinary company.
neighbors.shared: the deepest path leads back to your neighbors.
neighbors.sources: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 2:4 (paraphrase; 2:5 in some editions)

neighbors.heading: that nothing be lost
neighbors.text: Today not a grain of rice was left to throw away. In the Gospel of John, after Jesus feeds a crowd with five loaves, he says: "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost." Many Christians pause before eating to say grace, thanking God for the food.
neighbors.difference: Christians thank God for food as his gift, and the leftovers in the story point to his abundance. Oryoki's care is about noticing how much is enough, and some of the water goes to hungry beings, with no God to thank.
neighbors.shared: food is a gift, so none of it is wasted.

neighbors.heading: be not prodigal
neighbors.text: Today one raised hand said enough. The Qur'an asks for that same measure at the table: "eat and drink, but be not prodigal. Lo! He loveth not the prodigals." Muslims begin a meal in God's name, and the Prophet's way includes not wasting food, even a fallen bite.
neighbors.difference: For Muslims, eating with measure is gratitude and obedience to God, who provides. In oryoki, the measure is a practice of attention, and the meal's verses honor the work that brought the food, not a Creator.
neighbors.shared: knowing what's enough is its own kind of thanks.

neighbors.heading: o my soul
neighbors.text: Today Ruiyan called himself by name each day and answered yes. A psalm in the Church's prayer does something close: the singer talks to himself. "Why art thou sad, O my soul? and why dost thou trouble me? Hope in God." Not scolding. Just turning back.
neighbors.difference: The psalmist turns his soul toward God, in hope. Ruiyan's call simply wakes up attention, and the koan even asks who it is that answers; there is no God to hope in.
neighbors.shared: sometimes the kindest voice to wake you is your own.

neighbors.heading: o my mind
neighbors.text: Today a monk called to his own mind: wake up, don't be fooled. Gurbani speaks to the mind like that often. Guru Amar Das says: O my mind, you are a form of the divine light; know where you came from. It's a call home, made gently, to oneself.
neighbors.difference: Guru Amar Das calls the mind back to the light of the one God, its source. The koan leaves the caller and the one who answers open, and Wumen warns against taking any mask as the real self.
neighbors.shared: a gentle call to yourself can wake you up.
